newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican state votes on Sunday in test for ruling party.
newsitem.headline: Mexican state votes on Sunday in test for ruling party.

text.p: Voters in a rural state south of Mexico's capital will elect mayors and a state legislature on Sunday, testing the strength of President Ernesto Zedillo's party ahead of key midterm elections in July.
Voters gave Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) a drubbing at the polls in 1995 and 1996, punishing it for the country's dire economic crisis and numerous corruption scandals.

But PRI officials hope that this year with the economy recovering and the government party campaigning more vigorously under an aggressive new national leader, they can turn the tide against the opposition.

Reforma newspaper on Thursday published the results of its own poll in the three biggest municipalities in Morelos -- the state that votes on Sunday -- showing that the race was likely to be very close.

In the Morelos state capital Cuernavaca, Reforma said 25 percent of respondents planned to vote for the conservative National Action Party (PAN) against 24 percent for the PRI. The left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) trailed with 17 percent.
The poll also put the PAN ahead of the PRI in Morelos's second city of Jiutepec but the PRI led in the third biggest town, Cuautla, Reforma added.
It said 1,500 voters were surveyed between March 8 and 10. No margin of error was given.
With 893,000 registered voters, Morelos is one of Mexico's smaller states but its proximity to Mexico City gives it a higher political profile than its size might suggest.
The PRI state governor, Jorge Carrillo Olea, has recently been in the headlines after the New York Times reported he had links to drugs traffickers -- which he denied.

Carrillo's government has also suffered from citizen protests against a wave of kidnappings in the state. Victims have included middle-class professionals as well as the wealthy, and there have been accusations that state detectives were involved in some of the crimes.

Once home to peasant leader Emiliano Zapata, who led a revolt during the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution, Morelos is today better known as the state that press reports said contains two homes of the country's most wanted drug lord, Amado Carrillo Fuentes.
